Left: the alternate edges A-B, C-D, and E-F pair up every node, so is_perfect_matching() returns True. Right: only A-B and C-D, which leave E and F (filled in the accent color) unmatched, so is_perfect_matching() returns False." width="100%"} A perfect matching pairs up every node of the graph: it is a matching (no two edges share an endpoint) that touches all nodes. Only graphs with an even number of nodes can have one. Perfect matchings are what you want when nobody may be left out, such as assigning roommates, pairing chess players for a round, or covering a board with dominoes. Edge direction is ignored, and self-loops cannot be part of a matching. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [edges]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A list of integer edge IDs, such as the output of `maximum_weight_matching()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the edges exist, form a matching, and cover every node. Unknown edge IDs give `False`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A matching is perfect exactly when it has $V / 2$ edges, so the check validates the matching and counts its endpoints in $O(V + E)$ time. Whether a graph *has* a perfect matching can be decided by computing a maximum matching (`maximum_weight_matching()` on an unweighted graph) and checking it with this method. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A 6-cycle has two perfect matchings, made of alternate edges: ::: {#07ca5bfa .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec ring = ec.Graph().add_nodes(list("ABCDEF")) ring.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "A")]) alternate = [ring.find_edge_ids(u, v)[0] for u, v in [("A", "B"), ("C", "D"), ("E", "F")]] # Returns (True, False): dropping one edge leaves E and F unmatched ring.is_perfect_matching(alternate), ring.is_perfect_matching(alternate[:2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: ::: A maximum matching tells you whether a perfect one exists. A star never has one: ::: {#364d13d9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} star = ec.Graph().add_star_graph(4) star.is_perfect_matching(star.maximum_weight_matching()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: :::
